text: In the rivers of Africa lives an animal that looks lazy, round, almost comical.
It spends its days half asleep in the water. It eats grass. It has never hunted anything in its life.
And yet it is one of the most dangerous animals on the continent.
This is the hippopotamus. And almost everything you think you know about it is wrong.
Its name comes from ancient Greek: hippos, horse, and potamos, river. The river horse.
But a hippo is not a horse, and not even close. Its nearest living relatives are whales and dolphins.
More than fifty million years ago, they shared a common ancestor. The whales went to the sea. The hippos stayed by the river.
And it is enormous. A big bull can weigh around three tonnes.
say: And it is enormous. A big bull can weigh around three tonnes.

v.label: kilograms: the weight of a big bull

text: On land, only elephants and the largest rhinos outweigh it.
Its skin is thick, but it loses water fast. A hippo can't stay out in the hot sun for long.
So hippos spend most of the day in rivers and lakes, often up to sixteen hours.
Here's the strange part. Hippos can't really swim.
They are too dense to float. Instead, they walk along the bottom, or push off it in slow, bouncing leaps.
A hippo can hold its breath for about five minutes. Its ears and nostrils snap shut under water.
Even asleep, it rises to the surface to breathe, without waking up.
And then there's the so-called blood sweat.
Hippos ooze a red and orange liquid from their skin. It isn't blood, and it isn't really sweat.
In 2004, Japanese scientists found two pigments in it. Together, they work as a natural sunscreen, and they kill bacteria.
say: In two thousand and four, Japanese scientists found two pigments in it. Together, they work as a natural sunscreen, and they kill bacteria.

v.sub: Hippo “sweat”: a sunscreen and an antibiotic

text: When the sun goes down, the river horse becomes a land animal.
At dusk, hippos leave the water and walk inland to graze, often for several kilometres, along the same paths night after night.
In one night, an adult can eat around thirty-five kilograms of grass.

v.label: kilograms of grass in a single night
v.sub: mostly short grasses, cropped with the lips

text: By sunrise, it is back in the water. And that is where the grass ends up.
In Kenya's Mara River, about four thousand hippos add roughly eight and a half tonnes of dung to the water every day.
That dung feeds fish and insects downstream. But when the river runs low, it rots, strips the water of oxygen, and can kill the fish.
Hippos don't just live in the river. They shape it.

v.text:
They don't just live in the river.
They shape it.

text: So how does a grass eater become one of Africa's deadliest animals?
The answer is territory.
A dominant bull controls a stretch of river, and he defends it against rivals, crocodiles, boats, and people.
That huge yawn is not tiredness. It's a warning.
The jaws open to around one hundred and fifty degrees, showing tusks that can grow to half a metre and sharpen themselves as they grind together.
Its bite is often reported at around eighteen hundred pounds per square inch, strong enough to bite through a wooden canoe.

v.label: psi: a hippo's reported bite force
v.sub: measured on females; bulls are too dangerous to test

text: And on land, this three-tonne animal can sprint at around thirty kilometres an hour. Faster than most people can run.
Most attacks happen when people get between a hippo and the water, or when a boat surprises one in the shallows.
No one keeps exact records, but hippos are often estimated to kill around five hundred people in Africa every year.

v.label: people killed each year
v.sub: a widely quoted estimate; exact numbers are unknown

text: Hippos live in groups called pods, usually ten to thirty animals, ruled by a single territorial bull.
Fights between bulls can be brutal. Rivals slam their open mouths together and slash with their tusks. Some fights end in death.
Bulls also mark their territory in a way only a hippo could. They spin their tails like a propeller, and spray their dung.
After about eight months, a female gives birth, often in the water. The calf weighs between twenty-five and fifty kilograms.
It can suckle under water, and it often rests on its mother's back.
Mothers are fiercely protective, because calves have real enemies. Lions, hyenas, and crocodiles all go after young hippos.
A grown hippo has almost nothing to fear. Even a big crocodile usually keeps its distance.
For all its power, the hippo is in trouble.
Hippos once lived along the Nile and across most of sub-Saharan Africa. Today their range is broken into scattered pockets.
The IUCN estimates that between one hundred and fifteen thousand and one hundred and thirty thousand remain, and lists the species as vulnerable.

v.sub: common hippos left in the wild · IUCN: Vulnerable

text: Their rivers are dammed and drained for farms, and they are hunted for their meat, and for the ivory in their teeth.
Wherever there is a river in Africa, people and hippos have to share it. And that is not always easy.
So the next time you see a hippo yawning in the sun, remember what you are really looking at.
Not a lazy giant. A river engineer, a devoted mother, and the true ruler of Africa's rivers.
